```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%",
                      fig.alt = "A plot drawn by plot() on a cv.bregsurv fit of the discrete-time model.")
```

The framework does not fix the target model. This page covers the two targets beyond the Cox model:
the grouped-time model of an outcome recorded in intervals, and a neural-network risk score. Both enter
the same objective, $-\ell(\theta) + \eta\,\mathcal{B}_G(\theta)$.

## The grouped-time model

Subject $i$ is at risk in intervals $1, \dots, t_i$; the event, if any, happens in interval $t_i$. The
hazard of interval $k$ is

$$
h_{ik} = g^{-1}\!\left(\gamma_{s(i)k} + \mathbf z_i^\top \boldsymbol\beta\right),
$$

with one baseline parameter $\gamma_{sk}$ per stratum and interval and the complementary log-log link
(`link = "cloglog"`, the grouped proportional-hazards model, whose $\boldsymbol\beta$ has the meaning
of a Cox model's) or the logit link. The log-likelihood is a Bernoulli likelihood over the
person-intervals at risk. An interval in which no training subject has the event has a
maximum-likelihood hazard of zero; its baseline parameter is held at a floor corresponding to a hazard of
$10^{-8}$ instead of diverging.

`ExampleData_discrete` holds a cohort of 150 subjects followed for six intervals, an independent test
cohort, and a registry: its records, and the model it published from them.

```{r}
library(BregSurv)
data(ExampleData_discrete)
tr <- ExampleData_discrete$train
table(last_interval = tr$interval, event = tr$status)

target <- target_discrete(interval = tr$interval, event = tr$status, z = tr$z)
target
```

## The three divergences on a discrete target

**Kullback--Leibler: absolute risk.** The divergence is taken between the external and target hazards
of every interval at risk. It reduces to the Bernoulli likelihood with each outcome replaced by a soft
target, $(y_{ik} + \eta\,\tilde h_{ik})/(1+\eta)$, exactly as the Cox estimator replaces each event
indicator; this is the method of @wang2025discretekl. It needs the external model's interval hazards
$\tilde h_{ik}$, which a Cox model gives together with its baseline hazard, so the release is
`release_model()`: the coefficients with the baseline cumulative-hazard increments over your intervals,
or the interval hazards themselves (`hazard =`, one row per subject).

```{r}
registry_model <- release_model(beta = ExampleData_discrete$beta_external,
                                baseline = ExampleData_discrete$baseline_external)
fit_kl <- cv.bregsurv(target, registry_model, divergence = "kl")
plot(fit_kl)
```

A coefficient vector alone says nothing about interval hazards, so `release_coef()` cannot inform this
divergence on a discrete target.

**Mahalanobis.** Under the complementary log-log link the coefficients compare directly with a Cox
model's, so the published coefficients and their precision matrix enter as for a Cox target:

```{r}
registry_coef <- release_coef(ExampleData_discrete$beta_external, Q = ExampleData_discrete$Q_external)
fit_m <- cv.bregsurv(target, registry_coef, divergence = "mahalanobis")
```

**Composite likelihood.** The registry's records, on the same intervals, enter with weight $\eta$ and
their own baseline parameters:

```{r}
ex <- ExampleData_discrete$external
registry_records <- release_records(ex$z, interval = ex$interval, event = ex$status)
fit_c <- cv.bregsurv(target, registry_records, divergence = "composite")
```

Every discrete-time fit is scored by the same criterion: the held-out negative log-likelihood per
subject of the grouped-time model, pooled over the folds. With the same `seed`, they share one
partition, so their values compare directly, together with your data alone:

```{r}
own <- cv.bregsurv(target)
round(c(your_data_alone = own$value, kullback_leibler = fit_kl$value,
        mahalanobis = fit_m$value, composite = fit_c$value), 4)
```

```{r, fig.height = 4.2}
plot(fit_m, type = "coefficients")
```

## The estimators behind the fits

`cv.bregsurv()` hands a linear discrete-time target to one of three families of estimators, parallel to
the Cox and nested case--control ones, and returns exactly their result:

| divergence | estimator | ridge | lasso / elastic net |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kullback--Leibler | `discretekl()`, `cv.discretekl()` | `discretekl_ridge()`, `cv.discretekl_ridge()` | `discretekl_enet()`, `cv.discretekl_enet()` |
| Mahalanobis | `discrete_MDTL()`, `cv.discrete_MDTL()` | `discrete_MDTL_ridge()`, `cv.discrete_MDTL_ridge()` | `discrete_MDTL_enet()`, `cv.discrete_MDTL_enet()` |
| composite likelihood | `discrete_indi()`, `cv.discrete_indi()` | `discrete_indi_ridge()`, `cv.discrete_indi_ridge()` | `discrete_indi_enet()`, `cv.discrete_indi_enet()` |

```{r}
fit_kl$engine
direct <- cv.discretekl(z = tr$z, delta = tr$status, interval = tr$interval,
                        beta = ExampleData_discrete$beta_external,
                        baseline = ExampleData_discrete$baseline_external,
                        etas = fit_kl$path$eta, seed = fit_kl$seed)
identical(direct$best$best_value, fit_kl$value)
```

They take the arguments of their Cox counterparts with `interval` in place of `time`. Fits use Fisher
scoring with the baseline parameters profiled out, and proximal Newton with coordinate descent under an
$\ell_1$ penalty, in C++. The objective is scaled per subject, as for the Cox estimators, so $\eta$ has
the same meaning on both targets.

Predictions are interval hazards or survival at the end of each interval:

```{r}
te <- ExampleData_discrete$test
round(predict(fit_kl, te$z[1:3, ], type = "survival"), 3)
```

## Neural-network risk scores

`score = nn_score()` replaces $\mathbf z^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ by a feed-forward network. Only the
Kullback--Leibler divergence is defined for it, since the other two compare coefficients. The neural
targets need the `torch` package, so the code below is not run here.

* On a **discrete target** the network outputs one logit per interval, a logistic-hazard model, trained
  on the soft targets above: the external model is distilled into the network, and $\eta = 0$ is the
  network trained on your data alone.
* On a **Cox target** the network outputs a risk score, trained on the partial likelihood with each event
  indicator blended with the external pseudo-event weight. It is scored by the same cross-validated
  partial-likelihood loss as the linear Cox fits, on the same folds, so a network and a linear model
  can be compared.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("torch"); torch::install_torch()   # once

spec <- nn_score(hidden = c(128, 128, 128, 128), dropout = 0.1)
target_nn <- target_discrete(interval = tr$interval, event = tr$status, z = tr$z, score = spec)
net <- cv.bregsurv(target_nn, registry_model)
net$eta; plot(net)
```

The training protocol: within each fold, an event-stratified 20% of the training part is held out for
early stopping, the covariates are standardized on the rest, and every candidate starts from the same
initialization. The learning rate is chosen first, at $\eta = 0$, then $\eta$; the final network is
trained on all the data for the median best epoch of the selected setting. The default network has four
residual blocks of width 128, each a linear layer, layer normalization, ReLU and dropout.

Networks are random even with a seed fixed, across platforms and versions of `torch`; on one machine and
one version, a fixed `seed` reproduces the fit.
